title: Running on empty
_README: Branching burnout-reflection flow. Curated content only. NOTE: burnout here means everyday depletion and over-extension, not a medical condition. This flow never diagnoses. Free-text nodes with scanForCrisis:true are checked by the crisis scanner before storing.

intro.body: Let's be straight: rest isn't a reward you earn after you've done enough. If you're running on empty, the goal here isn't to help you push harder — it's to find where the leak is. This is reflection, not medical advice; if you've felt persistently low or unwell, please talk to a professional.

whats_draining.prompt: Where's most of your energy actually going right now?

options.label: Meeting other people's needs and expectations
Too many commitments I said yes to
Holding everything to an exhausting standard
Worrying and replaying things in my head

others_probe.prompt: Whose approval are you most afraid of losing if you did less? Name them, honestly.

others_reframe.body: Here's the hard part: people who only value you at full output aren't valuing you — they're valuing your usefulness. The ones who actually care about you would rather have you intact than impressive. Depleting yourself to keep everyone happy quietly teaches them your limits don't exist.

overcommit_probe.prompt: Think about your last three yeses. How many were actually a no you couldn't say?

overcommit_reframe.body: Every yes is a no to something else — usually your own rest, focus, or the things only you can do. A calendar full of other people's priorities isn't a sign of being needed; it's a sign your boundaries have gone missing. The fix isn't doing it all faster.

meant_them_socratic.body: If you meant them all and you're still empty, the issue may not be what you said yes to but that nothing gets to refill you in between.

standards_probe.body: Holding everything to a maximum standard means you never get to feel done. Perfectionism doesn't produce excellence — it produces exhaustion plus the constant feeling of falling short. Some things deserve your best. Most things just need to be finished.

standards_socratic.body: Which task in front of you would be completely fine at 80%, if you let it?

worry_probe.body: Rumination feels productive — like if you think about it enough, you'll solve it. But replaying isn't problem-solving; it's the mind idling in high gear, burning fuel without moving. The tank empties either way.

worry_socratic.body: Of everything you're turning over, what's the one piece that's actually yours to act on — and what's just noise you can set down?

permission_to_rest.prompt: Finish this: 'If I fully believed rest was allowed, the first thing I'd stop doing this week is ______.'

rest_reframe.body: Read back what you wrote. You already know where the leak is. Recovering isn't about a big dramatic reset — it's about giving that one thing up, or shrinking it, on purpose.

burnout_action.prompt: Name one small, protective step for the next 72 hours. Something that gives energy back or stops a leak — not another task.
suggestions: Decline or postpone one commitment that isn't essential.
Protect a 30-minute block this week that's only for you, and defend it.
Let one task be 'good enough' on purpose and notice nothing breaks.
Tell one person you trust that you're running low — out loud.

close.body: You found the leak and picked one repair. That's enough for today — genuinely. Real recovery is a lot of small honest choices like this one, not a heroic push. And if the emptiness runs deeper than tiredness, please reach out to a professional or someone you trust.
